title: Jio Payment Solutions Launches Cross-Border Platform for Indian Exporters
excerpt: The Jio Financial Services unit won RBI authorization to operate as a cross-border payment aggregator, offering multi-currency virtual accounts that let exporters skip SWIFT and correspondent banking.
body:
• Jio Payment Solutions Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Financial Services, launched a cross-border payments platform on September 9, 2026, letting Indian exporters accept payments from global customers through virtual accounts, international cards, and local payment rails.
  • The launch follows authorization from the Reserve Bank of India to operate as a Payment Aggregator for Cross-Border (PA-CB) transactions, covering both exports and imports.
  • Multi-currency virtual accounts let overseas buyers pay in their own currency and preferred local method without navigating SWIFT or correspondent banking — aimed at exporters, online sellers, SaaS companies, freelancers, and creators.
  • JPSL says the platform covers about half of India's export footprint — including the U.S., U.K., Europe, UAE, Singapore, Malaysia, and Australia — with more corridors across Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East planned in the coming months.

India's small exporters have a new way to get paid from abroad. Jio Payment Solutions Limited (JPSL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Financial Services, on Wednesday announced the launch of a cross-border payments platform that lets Indian businesses accept international payments from global customers — via virtual accounts, international cards, and local payment rails — in a bid to make Indian exporters more competitive in global markets.

The launch follows the receipt of authorization from the Reserve Bank of India to operate as a Payment Aggregator for Cross-Border (PA-CB) transactions, covering both exports and imports, the company said in a statement. JPSL already operates as a payment aggregator for online and physical point-of-sale transactions; with the cross-border launch, it says it now offers a comprehensive payments suite spanning digital commerce, physical retail, and international e-commerce for permitted current-account transactions.

The problem: fragmented global collections

As more Indian businesses — including online sellers, digital businesses, freelancers, creators, and SaaS companies — sell to customers abroad, collecting money remains, in JPSL's words, "a fragmented and complex process." It often involves multiple partners, different currencies, extensive paperwork, and manual reconciliation — friction that falls hardest on small exporters that lack a treasury department.

JPSL's answer is a single platform for global collections that bundles compliance and settlement while letting businesses offer customers their preferred local payment option in each market. The core building block is a multi-currency virtual account infrastructure: an exporter in Surat or Bengaluru can quote a price in dollars, euros, or dirhams and let the buyer pay through familiar local rails, without either side having to navigate SWIFT transfers or correspondent banking. Compliance, reconciliation, and settlement are handled inside the platform.

Scale at launch and what's next

According to JPSL, the platform at launch covers roughly half of India's total export footprint — merchants selling to the United States, United Kingdom, Europe, the UAE, Singapore, Malaysia, and Australia can quote in local currencies and collect payments seamlessly. The company says it plans to add more local payment methods across Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East in the coming months, extending coverage to exporters whose buyers sit in those corridors.

The offering is pitched across company sizes, from MSMEs and emerging exporters to large digital enterprises, with integration options that include hosted checkout flows. For freelance developers, designers, and creators — a fast-growing segment of India's services exports — the appeal is the same as for goods exporters: fewer intermediaries between an invoice and a settled payment.

A crowded field for cross-border aggregators

Jio enters a market where several Indian fintechs already hold the same RBI authorization. Cashfree Payments, for instance, received its PA-CB license earlier and has built its business on cross-border collections for Indian exporters. JPSL's advantage is distribution: as part of the Jio ecosystem — which reaches hundreds of millions of telecom subscribers and millions of small merchants — it can bring cross-border capabilities to businesses that have never used an international payment aggregator before.

The RBI has been tightening and formalizing the cross-border payments framework over the past two years, and PA-CB authorization effectively turns JPSL into a regulated on-ramp between Indian exporters and the global financial system. That regulatory standing matters to risk-averse buyers and to the banks that ultimately settle the funds.

What to watch

The metrics that will decide whether this launch matters: how quickly JPSL can expand beyond the initial corridor footprint, whether pricing undercuts incumbents like Cashfree and global rails such as Stripe and PayPal on the exporter side, and how well the platform handles the compliance load — tax forms, invoicing standards, and FIRC documentation that exporters must produce for Indian regulators. If the platform can make international collections as simple as a domestic UPI transaction, it could pull a meaningful share of India's next wave of digital exporters into the Jio ecosystem.
